reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Suspect the syndrome in a patient who develops respiratory distress, neurological change, and a petechial rash one to three days after long-bone or pelvic fractures
The classic triad is hypoxaemia, neurological dysfunction, and a petechial rash, though not all three are always present
The petechial rash is characteristically distributed over the upper trunk, axillae, neck, and conjunctivae and is a helpful clue when present
It is largely a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, since no single test is confirmatory
Management is supportive, centred on maintaining oxygenation and ventilation and treating respiratory failure
Early fracture immobilisation and timely fixation reduce the risk of developing the syndrome
Consider alternative causes of the same picture, particularly pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, and evolving brain injury
reference.pathophysiology: Fat embolism syndrome typically follows fractures of long bones or the pelvis, or orthopaedic instrumentation, when marrow fat enters the venous circulation. A mechanical component arises as fat globules occlude pulmonary and systemic capillaries, while a biochemical component follows as circulating free fatty acids are released and produce a toxic inflammatory injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium. The result is impaired gas exchange resembling acute lung injury, cerebral microembolism causing confusion and reduced consciousness, and dermal capillary involvement producing the characteristic petechiae. Symptoms characteristically appear after a latent interval of roughly one to three days.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Chest imaging that may show diffuse infiltrates as lung injury evolves
Full blood count that may reveal thrombocytopenia and anaemia
Imaging to exclude pulmonary embolism when the diagnosis is unclear
Neuroimaging where cerebral involvement or alternative brain pathology is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly worsening hypoxaemia progressing towards acute respiratory distress syndrome
Deteriorating conscious level from cerebral involvement
New petechial rash with respiratory and neurological change after long-bone fracture
Haemodynamic instability suggesting massive embolic load
Failure to improve prompting reconsideration of pulmonary embolism or sepsis
reference.prognosis: Most cases are self-limiting with supportive care and resolve over days, but severe presentations with marked respiratory failure or cerebral involvement carry higher morbidity and can be fatal.
pitfalls: Attributing early hypoxaemia solely to the injury and missing the evolving syndrome
Assuming the absence of a rash excludes the diagnosis
Failing to exclude pulmonary embolism, which requires different treatment
Delaying fracture stabilisation, which increases risk
Over-investigating for a confirmatory test rather than supporting the patient
management: Provide supportive respiratory care with supplemental oxygen and escalation to lung-protective mechanical ventilation for hypoxaemic respiratory failure
Prevent the syndrome through early immobilisation and timely operative fixation of long-bone and pelvic fractures
Support cerebral and haemodynamic function with close neurological observation for confusion or reduced consciousness
Correct associated anaemia and thrombocytopenia and provide general critical-care supportive measures
Monitor oxygenation, neurological status and platelet count while excluding pulmonary embolism and other causes
Escalate to critical care for severe respiratory failure or cerebral involvement
